name: SQL Server

inputs.name: ca
inputs.label: CA certificate file (PEM) - only for a private CA such as AWS RDS or Azure; Enter to skip

paste.instance: a named instance (host\instance) is not read: give the host and the instance's TCP port with --set host=... --set port=... (SQL Server Configuration Manager shows the port)

access: SELECT on the schema, through a database user mapped to its login (Azure SQL Database: a contained user)

schema_check.statement: SELECT CASE WHEN SCHEMA_ID({v}) IS NOT NULL THEN 'ok' ELSE 'missing' END

tips: Names keep SQL Server's spelling, spaces included: quote them, e.g. SELECT "OrderID" FROM <schema>."Orders".
datetime arrives as TIMESTAMP(3), bit as BOOLEAN, money as DECIMAL(19,4).
notes: SQL Server login only; Windows authentication and Entra ID are not part of this connector.
Exasol tested the jre8 build of mssql-jdbc 13.4.0; it runs on the Java 17 container.

A CA (--set ca=<PEM file or bundle>) is checked by the kit's TLS helper class, named in the URL (trustManagerClass): mssql-jdbc reads trust only from a file, and on Exasol Personal no path reaches both the adapter (sandbox, /buckets) and the loader (/ of the database container, /exa/bucketfs). The helper trusts exactly the given certificates and checks the host name; it is compiled from setup/virtual-schemas/java/ by the database's own Java and staged beside the driver (a second JAR= for the loader). Verified against RDS SQL Server 2019.
Without ca, verify relies on the loader's own CA store, which is empty on Exasol Personal 2.3.0 (an absolute cacerts symlink outside its root): give a public CA's root with --set ca too.
